anti_patterns: Minting before custody is proven: issuing tokens without a signed custodian attestation or settled payment creates unbacked supply that breaks the 1:1 invariant from genesis

Raw ERC-20 with an off-chain spreadsheet allowlist: transfer checks that live outside the token contract are bypassable via direct contract calls and the ACT (Approved Controllable TransferFrom) gap where transferFrom skips sender verification

Check-then-act compliance wrappers: whitelisting the destination but never re-checking the sender inside transferFrom lets revoked or sanctioned holders route around the gate through an approved spender
Single-EOA agent/controller key: one phishing email away from arbitrary mint, freeze, or forcedTransfer over the whole registry; administrative power must sit behind multi-sig plus timelock

Treating the oracle as the legal link: an NAV or reserve-balance feed proves a number, not that token holders own the reserve or that the custodian will honor redemption — the last-mile legal/operational engineering is still required
Push distributions looping over holders: gas scales with holder count and the payout transaction bricks past a few hundred recipients; use pull-claims or merkle distributors

Anonymous fungibility that strips provenance: pooling fractions without retaining asset linkage (SPV series, audit hash, document version) recreates the abstraction-from-underlying failure that regulators ban in sector regimes
Promising liquidity by design: tokenization enables transfer, it does not create buyers; launching without a venue or market maker strands holders with transferable but unsellable tokens
avoid_when: The asset has no willing secondary venue or market maker and holders need exit liquidity, not just transferability
A single organization with trusted parties can run a database registry with no multi-party trust gap
The legal wrapper cannot be formed or the asset title cannot be cleanly isolated in an SPV or trust
Sub-second settlement finality is required and chain confirmation times cannot meet it
Transfer restrictions are so bespoke per holder that on-chain compliance modules cost more than off-chain transfer-agent processing
Regulators in the target jurisdiction prohibit fractional interests in the asset class
benefits: Fractional ownership: high-minimum assets split into small tickets without rebuilding the legal structure, widening the investor base
Programmable compliance: KYC, jurisdiction, holding-period, and concentration rules execute atomically at transfer time via canTransfer gates instead of manual transfer-agent review
Faster settlement: delivery-versus-payment in one atomic transaction replaces T+1/T+2 pipelines and eliminates settlement-window counterparty risk
Live cap table: token balances are the registry, so ownership, corporate actions, and reporting read from one source instead of reconciled spreadsheets
Automated lifecycle: dividends, splits, lockup expiry, and redemption run as contract logic with auditable events rather than back-office batches
24/7 transferability: permissioned but always-on secondary movement within eligibility rules, independent of market hours
Auditability: every issuance, transfer, freeze, and forced action emits events against an immutable ledger with document hashes anchored
best_practices: Model the full lifecycle (subscription, issuance, transfer, distribution, redemption, default, recovery) before writing any contract, and surface where legal action gates on-chain transitions
Separate issuance, compliance, and distribution into distinct modules so a rule change never requires redeploying balances
Gate mint on verifiable deposit: require custodian multisig attestation or settled-payment proof before issuance executes
Verify both sender and receiver identity inside every transfer path including transferFrom, closing the ACT bypass
Put agent/controller roles behind multi-sig with timelocks, and emit a data hash (legal-order reference) on every forcedTransfer for the audit trail
Prefer pull-claim or merkle-distributor payouts over push loops; snapshot balances at a fixed block
Hash-anchor SPV documents, valuations, and audit reports on-chain with versioning so holders can verify the current legal state
Reconcile on-chain supply against custodian statements and the off-chain register on a schedule, with alerting on any divergence
Support key recovery without re-KYC where the standard allows it (identity-bound rather than wallet-bound permissioning)
Commission an independent audit and run emergency drills (pause, freeze, forced transfer) on forked mainnet before launch
component_types: Token Contract: fungible, non-fungible, or multi-asset ledger representing fractional or whole claims on the SPV-held asset
Issuance/Redemption Controller: permissioned mint-on-deposit and burn-on-redemption logic with notice periods and partial/full redemption rules
Identity Registry: wallet-to-verified-identity resolver binding KYC, accreditation, and jurisdiction claims to addresses
Compliance Module: programmable transfer rules (jurisdiction allowlists, holding periods, investor caps, concentration limits) evaluated pre-transfer
Custody/SPV Adapter: legal wrapper holding title plus custodian attestation interface authorizing mint and release
NAV/State Oracle: authorized feed publishing valuations, reserve balances, coupon schedules, and servicing events on-chain
Distribution Engine: pro-rata dividend or interest payout via pull-claims, merkle proofs, or vault accrual
Registrar Sync: reconciliation service keeping the off-chain cap table and on-chain supply in agreement
context: Issuers need to represent ownership in illiquid real-world assets (real estate, private credit, treasuries, commodities, art, fund equity) as blockchain tokens that enable fractional ownership, programmable transfer rules, and automated lifecycle events. The asset itself stays off-chain, held by a Special Purpose Vehicle or trust; tokens are on-chain claims on that wrapper. The pattern applies when multiple investors must hold, transfer, and receive distributions against one custodied asset under securities regulation, and the system must keep legal title, custody state, and token state in agreement across issuance, trading, distribution, redemption, and recovery.
design_principles: Legal primacy: the SPV agreement defines rights; contracts encode and execute those terms, never invent them
No unbacked mint: totalSupply must never exceed verified reserves; issuance is a consequence of deposit, not an independent action
Compliance at transfer time: eligibility is evaluated on every state change, not cached from onboarding
Identity over wallet: permission attaches to a persistent identity record so key rotation does not mean re-KYC
Sovereign recourse: legal ownership supersedes possession, so regulated tokens expose audited forced-transfer and recovery paths
Minimal on-chain data: documents and PII stay off-chain with hashes anchored; only proofs and state live on ledger
Atomic settlement: payment and title movement settle in one transaction wherever delivery-versus-payment is offered

technology_stack: Solidity (ERC-20 base, ERC-3643 T-REX identity/compliance suite, ERC-1400 partitions, ERC-1155 multi-asset)
ONCHAINID identity registry with trusted-issuer claims
OpenZeppelin contracts and ERC-1967 proxy upgradeability
Chainlink or equivalent oracles for NAV, reserve, and servicing data
Safe multi-sig plus timelock for agent and admin roles
Fireblocks, Komainu, or Hex Trust institutional custody with MPC
Sumsub, Veriff, or Jumio KYC/AML provider integrations
Hyperledger Besu or public EVM chains (Ethereum, Polygon) as settlement layer
tradeoffs: Backing trust is off-chain: the chain cannot observe the vault, so every mint depends on custodian honesty plus audit attestations, reintroducing trusted parties
Permissioned transfers curb composability: recipient identity requirements block permissionless DeFi pooling unless venues are whitelisted as verified entities
Gas overhead per transfer: identity checks plus modular compliance on every movement cost more than plain ERC-20 and scale with rule complexity
Partitioned cap tables are expensive: per-tranche balance iteration in ERC-1400 style designs risks hitting block gas limits as complexity grows
Liquidity is not automatic: fractional transferability without a venue or market makers leaves holders with sellable-in-theory positions
Regulatory fragmentation: securities treatment, eligibility, and disclosure differ per jurisdiction, so compliance logic must be configurable per market rather than written once
Concentrated admin power: agent/controller roles that can mint, freeze, or force-transfer are high-value attack surface requiring multi-sig governance
Privacy tension: cap-table transparency exposes holdings; confidentiality needs extra zero-knowledge or off-chain layers
use_cases: Tokenized treasuries and money-market funds with mint-on-subscription and burn-on-redemption against custodied securities
Fractional commercial real estate where an SPV holds title and investors trade fungible equity shares with jurisdiction-gated transfers
Private credit notes with coupon distribution via pull-claim contracts and Rule 144 holding-period lockups enforced on-chain
Commodity vault receipts (gold, oil) with 1:1 mint-on-deposit attested by custodian multisig and audited reserve reports
Fractionalized high-value NFTs locked in a vault with fungible shares representing proportional ownership plus buyout mechanics
Employee or fund equity with vesting tranches modeled as partitions with distinct transfer rules per tranche
